metadata.title: A Theorem of Roe and Strichartz on homogeneous trees

nodes.name: Roe's theorem (characterization of the sine function)
nodes.statement: Let $\{f_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be a doubly infinite sequence of real-valued functions of a real variable with $\frac{d}{dx}f_{k}=f_{k+1}.$ In 1980, J. Roe \cite{R} proved that if there exists a constant $M>0$ such that $|f_{k}(x)|\leq M\text{ for all }n\text{ and }x$ then $f_{0}(x)=a\sin(x+\theta)$ for some $a,\theta\in\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Roe: a uniformly bounded doubly infinite sequence with $f_k'=f_{k+1}$ forces $f_0(x)=a\sin(x+\theta)$.
assumptions: there exists a constant $M>0$ such that $|f_{k}(x)|\leq M\text{ for all }n\text{ and }x$

nodes.name: Strichartz's theorem
nodes.statement: Let $\{f_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be a doubly infinite sequence of functions in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ satisfying $\Delta_{\mathbb{R}^{n}} f_{k}=f_{k+1}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $|f_{k}(x)|\leq M$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$, where $M$ is a real number. Then $\Delta_{\mathbb{R}^{n}} f_{0}=-f_{0}$.
nodes.statement_short: Strichartz: a uniformly bounded sequence on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $\Delta f_k=f_{k+1}$ forces $f_0$ to be a $(-1)$-eigenfunction of the Laplacian.
assumptions: $|f_{k}(x)|\leq M$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$, where $M$ is a real number

nodes.name: Strichartz's result on Heisenberg groups and hyperbolic 3-space
nodes.statement: Furthermore, Strichartz also proved that the above result holds for Heisenberg groups but fails for hyperbolic 3-space.

nodes.name: Homogeneous tree
nodes.statement: A homogeneous tree $\mathfrak{X}$ of degree $q+1$ is a connected graph with no loops such that every vertex is adjacent to $q+1$ other vertices.
differentia: every vertex is adjacent to $q+1$ other vertices

nodes.name: Distance on a homogeneous tree
nodes.statement: The distance $d(x,y)$ between two vertices $x$ and $y$ defined as the number of edges joining $x$ and $y$.

nodes.name: Natural Laplace operator (Laplacian) $\mathcal{L}$ on $\mathfrak{X}$
nodes.statement: The natural Laplace operator (or Laplacian) $\mathcal L$ on $\x$ is defined by \begin{equation}\mathcal Lf(x)=f(x)-\frac{1}{q+1}\sum\limits_{y:d(x,y)=1}f(y).\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The tree Laplacian averages $f$ over the $q+1$ neighbours: $\mathcal{L}f(x)=f(x)-\frac{1}{q+1}\sum_{d(x,y)=1}f(y)$.

nodes.name: Spherical function $\phi_z$ and the eigenvalue function $\gamma$
nodes.statement: Consider the spherical function $\phi_z$ which is a radial eigenfunction of the Laplacian with eigenvalue $\gamma(z),$ where $\gamma$ is an analytic function defined by the formula \begin{equation} \gamma(z)=1-\frac{q^{1/2+iz}+q^{1/2-iz}}{q+1}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\phi_z$ is the radial $\mathcal{L}$-eigenfunction with eigenvalue $\gamma(z)=1-(q^{1/2+iz}+q^{1/2-iz})/(q+1)$.

nodes.name: Counterexample to Strichartz's theorem on a homogeneous tree
nodes.statement: Note that the image of $S_1=\{z\in\C: |\Im z|\leq1/2\}$ under the map $\gamma$ is an elliptic region which intersects $\{w\in\mathbb{C}:|w|=1\}$ in infinitely many points. Assume $f_{k}(x)=\gamma(z_{1})^{k}\phi_{z_1}(x)+\gamma(z_{2})^{k}\phi_{z_2}(x)$ for some $z_1,z_2$ in $S_1$ such that $\gamma(z_1)\neq\gamma(z_2)$ and $|\gamma(z_1)|=|\gamma(z_2)|=1$. Since $\phi_z$ is uniformly bounded on $S_1$, $\{f_k\}$ satisfy all the hypothesis of the Theorem \ref{th2}, but $f_{0}$ fails to be an eigenfunction of $\mathcal{L}$.
nodes.statement_short: A sum of two spherical functions with $|\gamma(z_1)|=|\gamma(z_2)|=1$ satisfies all hypotheses of Strichartz's theorem, yet $f_0$ is not an eigenfunction.

nodes.name: Failure of Strichartz's result is caused by the $L^p$-spectrum
nodes.statement: A careful analysis of the above counterexample reveals that the failure of Strichartz's result on $\mathfrak{X}$ is mainly due to the spectrum of $\mathcal{L}$. It was also observed in \cite{KRS2} that failure of Strichartz results is rooted in the $p$-dependence of the $L^p-$spectrum of the Laplacian on the hyperbolic spaces. In \cite{KRS2} it was proved that the theorem indeed remains valid when uniform boundedness is replaced by uniform ``almost $L^p$ boundedness". Here it is worth mentioning that these size estimates arise naturally due to the behaviour of the Poisson transforms, which also acts as the eigenfunctions of $\mathcal{L}$ with the eigenvalues lying in the interior of the ellipse (\ref{equation 1.2}) (For details see \cite{KR}).
nodes.statement_short: The counterexample is a spectral phenomenon; replacing uniform boundedness by uniform ``almost $L^p$ boundedness'' restores the theorem.

nodes.name: Theorem A
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a measurable on $\mathfrak{X}$ and $z\in\R\setminus(\tau/2)\Z$. If there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{k}f\|_{L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ then $\mathcal{L}f\equiv\gamma(z)f$. In particular, there exists $F\in L^{2}(\Omega)$ such that $f\equiv\mathcal{P}_{z}F$.
nodes.statement_short: Weak-$L^2$ growth $\|\mathcal{L}^kf\|_{2,\infty}\le M|\gamma(z)|^k$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ forces $f$ to be a $\gamma(z)$-eigenfunction, and a Poisson transform of an $L^2(\Omega)$ function.
assumptions: Let $f$ be a measurable on $\mathfrak{X}$ and $z\in\R\setminus(\tau/2)\Z$.
there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{k}f\|_{L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$

nodes.name: Theorem A as an extension of Strichartz's result to trees
nodes.statement: Since $\gamma(z)\in \R$ whenever $z\in\R\setminus(\tau/2)\Z$, Theorem A can be thought of as a suitable extension of Strichartz's result on homogeneous tree. In particular if we define $f_{k}=\gamma(z)^{-k}\mathcal{L}^{k}f$, then the statement of Theorem A resembles Theorem \ref{th2} with the only difference that the $L^{\infty}$ boundedness is being replaced by weak $L^{2}$ boundedness.
nodes.statement_short: With $f_k=\gamma(z)^{-k}\mathcal{L}^kf$, Theorem A is Strichartz's theorem with $L^\infty$ replaced by weak $L^2$.

nodes.name: Theorem B
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a measurable on $\mathfrak{X}$ and $1<p<2$. \begin{enumerate} \item Suppose that $z=n\tau+i\delta_{p'}$ for some $n\in\mathbb{Z}$. If there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{k}f\|_{L^{p^{\prime},\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ then $\mathcal{L}f\equiv\gamma(z)f$. \item Suppose that $z=(2n+1)\tau/2+i\delta_{p'}$ for some $n\in\mathbb{Z}$. If there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{-k}f\|_{L^{p^{\prime},\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{-k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ then $\mathcal{L}f\equiv\gamma(z)f$. \end{enumerate} In either of these cases, there exists $F\in L^{p^{\prime}}(\Omega)$ such that $f\equiv\mathcal{P}_{z}F$.
nodes.statement_short: For $1<p<2$ and $z$ on the boundary $\partial S_p$, one-sided weak-$L^{p'}$ growth of $\mathcal{L}^{\pm k}f$ already forces $f$ to be a $\gamma(z)$-eigenfunction given by a Poisson transform.
assumptions: Let $f$ be a measurable on $\mathfrak{X}$ and $1<p<2$.
there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{k}f\|_{L^{p^{\prime},\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$
there exists an $M>0$ such that $\|\mathcal{L}^{-k}f\|_{L^{p^{\prime},\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{-k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$
conclusions: In either of these cases, there exists $F\in L^{p^{\prime}}(\Omega)$ such that $f\equiv\mathcal{P}_{z}F$.

nodes.name: Poisson representation of weak $L^p$ eigenfunctions
nodes.statement: It was proved in \cite{KR} that any weak $L^p$ eigenfunction of the Laplacian of $\mathfrak{X}$ can be represented by the Poisson transform of a $L^{p}$ function on the boundary.
assumptions: any weak $L^p$ eigenfunction of the Laplacian of $\mathfrak{X}$
conclusions: can be represented by the Poisson transform of a $L^{p}$ function on the boundary

nodes.name: Sharper conclusion than Strichartz's theorem
nodes.statement: Therefore the conclusion of these theorems is more precise than that of Theorem \ref{th2}.

nodes.name: Isometry group $G$, stabilizer $K$, and radial functions
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be the group of isometries of the metric space $(\x,d)$ and let $K$ be the stabilizer of $o$ in $G$. The map $g\rightarrow g\cdot o$ identifies $\x$ with the coset space $G/K$, so that functions on $\x$ corresponds to $K$-right invariant functions on $G$. Further radial functions on $\x$ corresponds to $K$-bi-invariant functions on $G$. If $E(\x)$ is a function space on $\x$ we will denote by $E(\x)^\#$ the radial functions in $E(\x)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathfrak{X}\cong G/K$, radial functions correspond to $K$-bi-invariant functions, and $E(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ denotes the radial elements of $E(\mathfrak{X})$.

nodes.name: Infinite geodesic ray and the boundary $\Omega$ of $\mathfrak{X}$
nodes.statement: An infinite geodesic ray $\omega$ in $\x$ is an one-sided sequence $\{\omega_{n}: n=0,1,2\ldots \}$ where $\omega_n$'s are in $\x$. Let $o$ be some arbitrarily fixed point in $\x$. The boundary of $\x$ is the set of all infinite geodesic rays starting at $o$ and will be denoted by $\Omega$.
nodes.genus: the set of all infinite geodesic rays starting at $o$

nodes.name: Poisson kernel $p(x,\omega)$
nodes.statement:
Let $
u$ be the $G$-quasi-invariant probability measure on the boundary $\Omega$. The Poisson kernel $p(g\cdot o,\omega)$ is the Radon-Nikodym derivative $d
u(g^{-1}\omega)/d
u(\omega)$ and explicitly written as $$ p(x,\omega)=q^{h_{\omega}(x)} \;\;  orall x\in \x \;\;  orall \omega\in\Omega,$$ where $h_{\omega}(x)$ is the height of $x$ in $\x$ with respect to $\omega$ (see \cite{FTC} for details).
nodes.statement_short: The Poisson kernel is the Radon-Nikodym derivative $d\nu(g^{-1}\omega)/d\nu(\omega)$, explicitly $q^{h_\omega(x)}$.

nodes.name: Poisson transformation $\mathcal{P}_z$
nodes.statement: The Poisson transformation $\mathcal{P}_{z}:C(\Omega)\rightarrow C(\x)$ is given by the formula $$\mathcal{P}_{z}\eta(x)=\int\limits_{\Omega}p^{1/2+iz}(x,\omega)\eta(\omega)d\nu(\omega).$$

nodes.name: Period $\tau$ and the torus $\mathbb{T}$
nodes.statement: It is obvious that $\mathcal{P}_{z}=\mathcal{P}_{z+\tau}$, where $\tau=2\pi/\log q$. We denote the torus $\R/\tau \Z$ by $\mathbb{T}$, which can be identified with the interval $[-\tau/2,\tau/2)$.

nodes.name: Poisson transforms are eigenfunctions of $\mathcal{L}$
nodes.statement: It is a well-known fact that $\mathcal L \mathcal{P}_{z}\eta(x) =\gamma(z) \mathcal{P}_{z}\eta(x)$ for every $z$ in $\mathbb{C},$ where expression of $\gamma(z)$ is given in (\ref{eq01}).

nodes.name: Elementary spherical function $\phi_z$
nodes.statement: The elementary spherical function $\phi_z$ on $\mathfrak X$ is the Poisson transform of the constant function $\mathbf{1}$.
nodes.genus: the Poisson transform of the constant function $\mathbf{1}$

nodes.name: $\phi_z$ is the normalized radial eigenfunction
nodes.statement: Note that $\phi_z$ is the radial eigenfunction of $\mathcal L$ with eigenvalue $\gamma(z)$ such that $\phi_z(o)=1$.
conclusions: $\phi_z$ is the radial eigenfunction of $\mathcal L$ with eigenvalue $\gamma(z)$ such that $\phi_z(o)=1$

nodes.name: Radialization $\varepsilon f$
nodes.statement: For a suitable function $f$ on $\mathfrak{X}$, its radialization $\varepsilon f$ is defined as \begin{equation} \varepsilon f(x)=\int\limits_{K}f(k\cdot x)dk, \end{equation} where $dk$ is the normalized measure on $K$.

nodes.name: Useful facts about radialization
nodes.statement: Some useful facts about radialization: \begin{enumerate} \item $\|\varepsilon f\|_{p,q}\leq\|f\|_{p,q}$ whenever $1<p<\infty$, $1\leq q\leq\infty$. \item The operator $\varepsilon$ commutes with the Laplacian $\mathcal{L}$, that is $\mathcal{L}(\varepsilon f)=\varepsilon(\mathcal{L}f).$ \item Also if $\mathcal L u=\gamma(z)u$ then $\varepsilon u (x)=u(o)\phi_z(x)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Radialization is Lorentz-norm contractive, commutes with $\mathcal{L}$, and sends a $\gamma(z)$-eigenfunction $u$ to $u(o)\phi_z$.
conclusions: The operator $\varepsilon$ commutes with the Laplacian $\mathcal{L}$, that is $\mathcal{L}(\varepsilon f)=\varepsilon(\mathcal{L}f).$
Also if $\mathcal L u=\gamma(z)u$ then $\varepsilon u (x)=u(o)\phi_z(x)$.

nodes.name: Explicit expression of the spherical function $\phi_z$
nodes.statement: The following expression of the function $\phi_z$ is well-known (see \cite{FTP1}) \begin{equation} \phi_z(x)= \begin{cases} \vspace*{.2cm} \left(\frac{q-1}{q+1}|x|+1\right)q^{-|x|/2}&\forall z\in\ \tau\Z\\ \vspace*{.2cm}\left(\frac{q-1}{q+1}|x|+1\right)q^{-|x|/2}(-1)^{|x|}&\forall z\in {\tau/2}+\tau\Z\\ \mathbf{c}(z)q^{{(iz-1/2)}|x|}+\mathbf{c}(-z)q^{{(-iz-1/2)}|x|}&\forall z\in\C\setminus(\tau/2)\Z, \end{cases} \end{equation} where $\mathbf{c}$ is a meromorphic function given by $$\mathbf{c}(z)=\frac{q^{1/2}}{q+1}\frac{q^{1/2+iz}-q^{-{1/2}-iz}}{q^{iz}-q^{-iz}}\quad\forall z\in (\tau/2)\Z.$$
nodes.statement_short: Case formula for $\phi_z$ on $\tau\mathbb{Z}$, $\tau/2+\tau\mathbb{Z}$ and elsewhere, in terms of the meromorphic $\mathbf{c}$-function.
conclusions: where $\mathbf{c}$ is a meromorphic function given by $$\mathbf{c}(z)=\frac{q^{1/2}}{q+1}\frac{q^{1/2+iz}-q^{-{1/2}-iz}}{q^{iz}-q^{-iz}}\quad\forall z\in (\tau/2)\Z.$$

nodes.name: Uniform bound $|\phi_z|\leq 1$ on the strip $S_1$
nodes.statement: It is easy to verify that $|\phi_{z}(x)|\leq 1$ for all $x\in\x$ whenever $z\in S_1=\{z\in\C: |\Im z|\leq1/2\}$.

nodes.name: The parameters $\delta_p$ and the strips $S_p$
nodes.statement: Now we give some $L^p-$type estimates of $\phi_{z}(x)$. For $p\in(1,\infty)$ we define $$\delta_p=\frac{1}{p}-\frac{1}{2}\;\;\; \text{and}\;\;\; S_p=\{z\in\C: |\Im z|\leq|\delta_p|\}.$$ It is important to note that $\delta_p=-\delta_{p^{\prime}}$ and $S_{2}=\mathbb{R}$. We assume $\delta_1=-\delta_\infty=1/2$ so that $S_1=\{z\in\C: |\Im z|\leq1/2\}$. We shall henceforth write $S_p^\circ$ and $\partial{S_p}$ to denote the usual interior and boundary of $S_p$ respectively.
nodes.statement_short: $\delta_p=1/p-1/2$ and $S_p=\{z:|\Im z|\le|\delta_p|\}$, with $S_2=\mathbb{R}$ and $\delta_1=1/2$.

nodes.name: $L^{p'}$ and Lorentz norm estimates of $\phi_z$
nodes.statement: Let $1<p<2$. Then \begin{enumerate} \item[$1.$] $\phi_z\in L^{p'}(\x)\quad\text{if and only if}\quad z\in S_p^\circ$ \item[$2.$] $\phi_z\in L^{p',\infty}(\x)\quad\text{if and only if}\quad z\in S_p.$ \item[$3.$] $\phi_z\notin L^{2,\infty}(\x)$ if $z\in(\tau/2)\Z$ and $\phi_z\in L^{2,\infty}(\x)$ if $z\in\R\setminus(\tau/2)\Z$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $\phi_z\in L^{p'}$ iff $z\in S_p^\circ$, $\phi_z\in L^{p',\infty}$ iff $z\in S_p$, and $\phi_z\in L^{2,\infty}$ exactly off $(\tau/2)\mathbb{Z}$.
conclusions: $\phi_z\in L^{p'}(\x)\quad\text{if and only if}\quad z\in S_p^\circ$
$\phi_z\in L^{p',\infty}(\x)\quad\text{if and only if}\quad z\in S_p.$

nodes.name: $\gamma(S_p^\circ)$ lies in the point spectrum of $\mathcal{L}$
nodes.statement: From the above lemma it is clear that $\gamma(S_p^\circ)$ lies in the point spectrum of the $\mathcal L,$ which is a bounded operator on $L^{p^\prime}(\mathfrak X)$.
conclusions: $\gamma(S_p^\circ)$ lies in the point spectrum of the $\mathcal L,$ which is a bounded operator on $L^{p^\prime}(\mathfrak X)$

nodes.name: The $L^p$-spectrum $\sigma_p(\mathcal{L})$ of the Laplacian
nodes.statement: For every $p\in[1,\infty]$, the $L^{p}$-spectrum $\sigma_{p}(\mathcal{L})$ of $\mathcal{L}$ is the image of $S_p$ under the map $\gamma$, which is precisely the set of all $w$ in $\mathbb{C}$ which satisfies \begin{equation} \left[\frac{1-\Re(w)}{b\cosh(\delta_{p}\log q)}\right]^{2}+\left[\frac{\Im(w)}{b\sinh(\delta_{p}\log q)}\right]^{2}\leq 1,\text{ where }b=\frac{2\sqrt{q}}{q+1}. \end{equation} In particular, $\sigma_{2}(\mathcal{L})$ degenerates into the line segment $[1-b,1+b]$.
nodes.statement_short: $\sigma_p(\mathcal{L})=\gamma(S_p)$ is an elliptic region; for $p=2$ it degenerates to the segment $[1-b,1+b]$.
conclusions: In particular, $\sigma_{2}(\mathcal{L})$ degenerates into the line segment $[1-b,1+b]$.

nodes.name: Spherical Fourier transform $\hat{f}$
nodes.statement: The spherical Fourier transform $\hat{f}$ of a finitely supported radial function $f$ is defined by \begin{equation} \hat{f}(z)=\sum\limits_{x\in\x}f(x)\phi_z(x)\quad\text{ where }z\in\C. \end{equation}

nodes.name: $\hat{f}$ is even and $\tau$-periodic
nodes.statement: The symmetric properties of the spherical function implies that $\hat{f}$ is even and $\tau$-periodic on $\mathbb{C}$.

nodes.name: The $p$-Schwartz space $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$
nodes.statement: For $1<p\leq 2$, we define the space $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$ which consists of all those functions $f$ defined on $\mathfrak{X}$ such that \begin{equation} \nu_{m}(f)=\sup\limits_{x\in\mathfrak{X}}(1+|x|)^{m}q^{|x|/p}|f(x)|<\infty,\text{ for all }m\in\mathbb{N}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$ collects functions with all seminorms $\nu_m(f)=\sup_x(1+|x|)^mq^{|x|/p}|f(x)|$ finite.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$ is a Fréchet space of rapidly decreasing functions
nodes.statement: It is known that $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$ form Fr\'{e}chet space with respect to these countable seminorms $\nu_{m}(\cdot)$ and are also known as the $p$-Schwartz spaces of rapidly decreasing functions on $\mathfrak{X}$ (see \cite{CMS}).
conclusions: $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$ form Fr\'{e}chet space with respect to these countable seminorms $\nu_{m}(\cdot)$

nodes.name: The space $\mathcal{H}(S_p)^{\#}$
nodes.statement: For $1<p\leq 2$, we also define the space $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$ of all even, $\tau$-periodic function $g$ on $S_{p}$ which are holomorphic on $S_{p}^{\circ}$, continuous on $\partial S_{p}$ and satisfies \begin{equation} \mu_{m}(g)=\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}}\left|\frac{d^m}{dz}g(z)\right|<\infty,\text{ for all }m\in\mathbb{N}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{H}(S_p)^{\#}$ consists of even $\tau$-periodic functions holomorphic on $S_p^\circ$, continuous up to $\partial S_p$, with all derivative seminorms finite.

nodes.name: Isomorphism theorem for the spherical Fourier transform on $\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$
nodes.statement: It was proved in \cite{JF} that the spherical Fourier transform is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ onto $\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$.
conclusions: the spherical Fourier transform is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ onto $\mathcal{H}(S_{2})^{\#}$

nodes.name: The analogous isomorphism for $1<p<2$ is proved in the appendix
nodes.statement: In fact a similar result also holds when we consider $1<p<2$. The proof is given in appendix.

nodes.name: $L^p$-tempered distribution
nodes.statement: For $1<p\leq 2$, a linear functional $T:\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})\rightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is said to be a $L^{p}$-tempered distribution if $\langle T,f_{n}\rangle\rightarrow 0$ whenever $\nu_{m}(f_{n})\rightarrow 0$ for all $m\in\mathbb{N}$.

nodes.name: Radial distribution
nodes.statement: The distribution $T$ is said to be radial if $$\langle T,f\rangle=\langle T,\varepsilon f\rangle,\text{ for all }f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X}).$$

nodes.name: Radial part $\varepsilon T$ of an $L^p$-tempered distribution
nodes.statement: In fact the radial part of an $L^{p}$-tempered distribution $T$ is again an $L^{p}$-tempered distribution defined by $$\langle\varepsilon T,f\rangle=\langle T,\varepsilon f\rangle,\text{ for all }f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X}).$$

nodes.name: Left translation $\tau_x T$ of a distribution
nodes.statement: The left translation $\tau_{x}$ of $T$ by an element $x\in G$ is defined as follow if $f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$ then $$\langle \tau_{x}T,f\rangle=T(\tau_{x^{-1}}f)=T\ast f^{\ast}(x^{-1})$$ where $f^{\ast}(x)=f(x^{-1})$.
nodes.definiendum: left translation $\tau_{x}$ of $T$ by an element $x\in G$

nodes.name: Spherical Fourier transform of a radial $L^p$-tempered distribution
nodes.statement: Finally, the spherical Fourier transform $\hat{T}$ of a radial $L^{p}$-tempered distribution $T$ is a linear functional on $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$ defined by the following rule: $$\langle \hat{T},\psi\rangle=\langle T,f\rangle,\text{ where }\psi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}\text{ and }\hat{f}=\psi.$$
nodes.definiendum: spherical Fourier transform $\hat{T}$ of a radial $L^{p}$-tempered distribution $T$

nodes.name: Strategy: Theorems A and B follow from three key lemmas
nodes.statement: Our approach is motivated by proof given in \cite{KRS2}, which in turn is influenced by Strichartz's approach. In both the papers, the Fourier transform of a tempered distribution played an important role. Proof of Theorem A and Theorem B is an immediate consequence of following three key results, namely, Lemma A, Lemma B1, and Lemma B2.

nodes.name: Set up the claim on the holomorphic side
nodes.statement: We prove the this result for radial distributions, while the general case follows in a similar way as in Theorem \ref{Theorem10}. For $p\in(1,2)$ let $z_{0}=i\delta_{p^{\prime}}$. For a fixed $N\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ we claim that $$(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\widehat{T_{0}}=0.$$ As observed earlier, for any $\phi\in\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$ we have, $$ |\langle(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\widehat{T_{0}},\phi\rangle|\leq M\mu\left[\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi\right)\right].$$
nodes.statement_short: Take $z_0=i\delta_{p'}$ and reduce to showing $(\gamma(z_0)-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\widehat{T_0}=0$ via the seminorm bound.

nodes.name: Reduce the seminorm to a supremum over the half-strip $S_p^+$
nodes.statement: Since $\gamma(z)$ and $\phi(z)$ are $\tau-$periodic, even functions on $S_{p}$, so the seminorm $\mu$ on $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$ is given by \begin{align*} \mu\left[\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi\right)\right]&=\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}}\left|\frac{d^{m}}{dz^{m}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|\\ &=\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}}\left|\frac{d^{m}}{dz^{m}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|\\ &=\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}} F_{k}(z)\text{ (say),} \end{align*} where $S_{p}^{+}=\{z\in S_{p}:~\; |\Re z|\leq \tau/2\;\; \text{and}\;\; \Im z\geq 0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Evenness and $\tau$-periodicity let $\mu$ be computed as $\sup_{S_p^+}F_k$.

nodes.name: Leibniz bound on $F_k$
nodes.statement: To prove our claim it is enough to show that $\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$. Now for all $z\in S_{p}^{+}$, \begin{align} F_{k}(z)&\leq\sum\limits_{i=0}^{m}\binom{m}{i}\left|\frac{d^{i}}{dz^{i}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}\right)\right| \left|\frac{d^{m-i}}{dz^{m-i}}\left((\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|\nonumber\\ &\leq\sum\limits_{i=0}^{m}\binom{m}{i}B_{m}\left|\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right|^{k}k(k+1)(k+2)\ldots(k+i-1)\\ &\hspace*{4.8cm}\times\left|\frac{d^{m-i}}{dz^{m-i}}\left((\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|.\nonumber \end{align} From above inequality we also have \begin{equation}F_{k}(z)\leq A_{m}k^{m}\left|\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right|^{k} \end{equation} where $A_{m}=\max\limits_{0\leq i\leq m}\left[\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}}\left|\frac{d^{i}}{dz^{i}}\left((\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1}\phi(z)\right)\right|\right].$ In the above calculation we have also used the following estimates. For every $z\in S_{p}^{+}$, \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] $\left|\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right|\leq 1$, \item[(ii)] $\left|\frac{d^{i}}{dz^{i}}\left(\left(\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right)^{k}\right)\right|\leq B_{m}\left|\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right|^{k}k(k+1)(k+2)\ldots(k+i-1)$, where $0\leq i\leq m$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Expand the $m$-th derivative by Leibniz and use $|\gamma(z_0)/\gamma(z)|\le1$ to get $F_k\le A_mk^m|\gamma(z_0)/\gamma(z)|^k$.

nodes.name: Split the half-strip into $V_k$ and its complement
nodes.statement: In order to prove that $\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}^{+}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$, it is enough to show that \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] $\sup\limits_{z\in V_{k}^{c}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$, \item[(b)] $\sup\limits_{z\in V_{k}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$. \end{enumerate} where for $k$ (large enough) $$V_{k}=\{z\in S_{p}^{+}: |\Re z|<(k^{1/4}\log q)^{-1}\text{ and } \delta_{p}-\log(1+1/k^{1/6})(\log q)^{-1}<\Im z\leq\delta_{p}\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the shrinking box $V_k$ around $i\delta_p$ and treat $V_k$ and $V_k^c$ separately.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B

nodes.name: Estimate on $V_k^c$
nodes.statement: First we deal with (a). In view of equation (\ref{eq31}), it is sufficient to show that for every $z\in V_{k}^{c}$ there exists a constant $c>0$ such that \begin{equation} \left|\frac{\gamma(z_{0})}{\gamma(z)}\right|^{k}\leq\left(1+\frac{c}{\sqrt{k}}\right)^{-k}. \end{equation} First case, if $0\leq \Im z\leq \delta_{p}-\frac{\log(1+1/k^{1/6})}{\log q}$ then $|\gamma(z)|\geq |\gamma(i(\delta_{p}-\frac{\log(1+1/k^{1/6})}{\log q}))|$. Hence \begin{align} |\gamma(z)|-|\gamma(z_{0})|&\geq \left(\frac{q^{1/p}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{q+1}\right)-\left(\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}\right)\nonumber\\ &=\frac{1}{q+1}\frac{q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{k^{1/6}(1+k^{1/6})}\left[k^{1/6}(q^{2/p-1}-1)-1\right]. \end{align} Since $q^{2/p-1}-1>0$, there exists $k_{0}\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $k^{1/6}(q^{2/p-1}-1)\geq 2$ for every $k\geq k_{0}$. This together with (\ref{eq33}) gives the desired inequality (\ref{eq32}). Other case if $z\in V_{k}^{c}$ is such that $\tau/2\geq|\Re z|\geq (k^{1/4}\log q)^{-1}$, then $$|\gamma(z)|\geq \left(1-\frac{q^{1/p^{\prime}}+q^{1/p}}{q+1}cos(k^{-1/4})\right)$$ and $$|\gamma(z)|-|\gamma(z_{0})|\geq\left(\frac{q^{1/p^{\prime}}+q^{1/p}}{q+1}(1-\cos(k^{-1/4}))\right)\geq \frac{c}{k^{1/2}}.$$ Thus for every $z\in V_{k}^{c}$, inequality (\ref{eq32}) holds. Eventually, $\sup\limits_{z\in V_{k}^{c}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: On $V_k^c$ show $|\gamma(z_0)/\gamma(z)|^k\le(1+c/\sqrt{k})^{-k}$, splitting into the two ways of leaving $V_k$.

nodes.name: Estimate on $V_k$
nodes.statement: Now let us assume that $z\in V_{k}$. Then $z=a+i\delta_{r}$, where $|a|<(k^{1/4}\log q)^{-1}$ and $\delta_{p}-\log(1+1/k^{1/6})(\log q)^{-1}<\delta_{r}\leq\delta_{p}$ and we have \begin{align*} |\gamma(z)-\gamma(z_{0})|^{2}&=\left(\frac{q^{1/p^{\prime}}+q^{1/p}}{q+1}-\frac{q^{1/r^{\prime}}+q^{1/r}}{q+1}\cos(a\log q)\right)^{2} +\left(\frac{q^{1/r}-q^{1/r^{\prime}}}{q+1}\right)^{2}\sin^{2}(a\log q)\\ &\leq \left(\frac{q^{1/p}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{q+1}-\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}\cos(k^{-1/4})\right)^{2}\\ &\hspace*{8cm}+\left(\frac{q^{1/p}-q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{q+1}\right)^{2}\sin^{2}(k^{-1/4}) \end{align*} It follows from the inequality $\sqrt{|x|^2+|y|^2}\leq |x|+|y|$ that \begin{align*} |\gamma(z)-\gamma(z_{0})|&\leq \left(\frac{q^{1/p}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{q+1}-\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}\cos(k^{-1/4})\right)+\frac{c_{1}}{k^{1/4}}\\ &= \left(\frac{q^{1/p}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}}{q+1}-\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}\right)\\ &\hspace*{3cm}+\frac{q^{1/p}(1+k^{-1/6})^{-1}+q^{1/p^{\prime}}(1+k^{-1/6})}{q+1}(1-\cos(k^{-1/4}))+\frac{c_{1}}{k^{1/4}}\\ &\leq \frac{c_{3}}{k^{1/6}}+\frac{c_{2}}{k^{1/2}}+\frac{c_{1}}{k^{1/4}}\leq\frac{c}{k^{1/6}}, \end{align*} where the constants $c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}$ (and hence $c$) are independent of $k$. If we take $N=7m+1$ then each term in equation (\ref{eq30}) atleast contains the factor $(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{N+1-m}=(\gamma(z_{0})-\gamma(z))^{6m+2}$. Thus from above estimates and equation (\ref{eq30}), we finally have $\sup\limits_{z\in V_{k}} F_{k}\leq \frac{C}{k^{1/3}},$ where $C$ is independent of $k$ and $\sup\limits_{z\in S_{p}} F_{k}\rightarrow 0$ as $k\rightarrow\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: On $V_k$ bound $|\gamma(z)-\gamma(z_0)|\le c k^{-1/6}$ and take $N=7m+1$, giving $\sup_{V_k}F_k\le Ck^{-1/3}$.

nodes.name: Conclude part (a)
nodes.statement: Using the same argument given in \cite{KRS2} one can easily prove that $N=0$. This completes the proof of part (a) for radial and eventually for general distributions.

nodes.name: Parts (b) and (c)
nodes.statement: The proof of part (b) is similar to that of part (b) Lemma A. To prove part (c), assume that $\gamma(\tau/2+i\delta_{p^{\prime}})>|\lambda|>\gamma(i\delta_{p^{\prime}})$. Then $\gamma(S_{p}^{\circ})$ intersects $\{w\in\C:|w|=|\lambda|\}$ at infinitely many points. nodes.name: Lemma B2
nodes.statement: For $1<p<2$, let $\{T_{-k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^+}$ be an infinite sequence of $L^p$-tempered distributions on $\mathfrak{X}$ satisfying, \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathcal{L}T_{-k}=\lambda T_{-k+1}$ for some non-zero $z\in\mathbb{C}$ and \item $|\langle T_{-k},\phi\rangle|\leq M\nu(\phi)$ for all $\phi\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$, where $\nu$ is some fixed semi-norm of $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})$ and $M>0$. \end{enumerate} Then we have the following results. \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] If $|\lambda|=\gamma(\tau/2+i\delta_{p^{\prime}})$, then $\mathcal{L}T_{0}=|z|T_{0}$ and \item[(b)] If $|\lambda|>\gamma(\tau/2+i\delta_{p^{\prime}})$, then $T_{-k}=0$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}^+$. \item[(c)] There are solutions which are not eigen-distributions whenever $\gamma(\tau/2+i\delta_{p^{\prime}})> |\lambda|>\gamma(i\delta_{p^{\prime}})$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Backward-index analogue of Lemma B1, with the threshold $\gamma(\tau/2+i\delta_{p'})$ replacing $\gamma(i\delta_{p'})$.

nodes.statement: Now we will conclude the rest of the proof of the our main theorems. Let $z_0=\gamma(z)$ for $z\in\R\setminus\tau/2\Z$. From the give assumption in Theorem A if we define $T_k=\gamma(z)^{-k}\mathcal L^k f$ then $T_k$ is a $L^2$-tempered distribution and the proof of the Theorem A is a consequence of the Lemma A. Similarly if we assume that $T_{k}=\gamma(i\delta_{p^{\prime}})^{-k}\mathcal{L}^{k}f$ where $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$. According to the hypothesis of Theorem B, $\|T_{k}\|_{p^\prime,\infty}\leq M$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$. It is easy to show that each $T_{k}$ is an $L^p$-tempered distribution which satisfies all the hypothesis of Lemma B1. Hence $\mathcal{L}f=\gamma(i\delta_{p^{\prime}})f$. This completes the proof of the 1st part of Theorem B. The remaining part of Theorem B will follow from the Lemma B2.

nodes.statement: The remaining part of Theorem B will follow from the Lemma B2.
nodes.statement_short: The backward-index case of Theorem B is Lemma B2.
nodes.section: 3 Proof of Theorem A and theorem B

nodes.name: Theorem A fails on $(\tau/2)\mathbb{Z}$
nodes.statement: Observe that if $\mathcal L u=\gamma(z)u$ for $z\in(\tau/2)\mathbb{Z}$ then $u\notin L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak{X})$. Assume $u(x_o)\neq 0$ for some $x_o\in \mathfrak X$. If $u\in L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak{X})$ then $f(x)=\int_Ku(x_okx)dk=u(x_o)\phi_z(x)$ also belong to $L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak{X})$. In view of Lemma \ref{phiz} this not true as $\phi_{z}$ does not belong to $L^{2,\infty}(\mathfrak{X})$ whenever $z\in(\tau/2)\mathbb{Z}$. This observation shows that Theorem A is no longer valid for any $z\in(\tau/2)\mathbb{Z}$. However if we replace the $L^{2,\infty}$ estimate by $\|\phi_{0}^{-1}\mathcal{L}^{k}f\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathfrak{X})}\leq M|\gamma(z)|^{k}$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, then Theorem A holds true.
nodes.statement_short: For $z\in(\tau/2)\mathbb{Z}$ no eigenfunction is in $L^{2,\infty}$, so Theorem A fails there, but a $\phi_0$-weighted $L^\infty$ estimate restores it.
nodes.section: 4 Sharpness of the main results and the case $q=1$

nodes.name: The Lorentz exponents in Theorems A and B cannot be improved
nodes.statement: It follows from equation (\ref{eqsf}) and Lemma \ref{phiz} that in Theorem A (resp. in Theorem B), the $L^{2,\infty}$ (resp. the $L^{p^{\prime},\infty}$) estimate cannot be replaced by $L^{2,r}$, $r<\infty$ (resp. $L^{q^{\prime},r}$ with $q>p$ or $L^{p^{\prime},r}$ with $r<\infty$). The proof is similar as above.
nodes.statement_short: The $L^{2,\infty}$ (resp. $L^{p',\infty}$) hypothesis cannot be weakened to $L^{2,r}$ with $r<\infty$ (resp. $L^{q',r}$ with $q>p$).
nodes.section: 4 Sharpness of the main results and the case $q=1$

nodes.name: All integral powers of $\mathcal{L}$ are needed in Theorem A
nodes.statement: Unlike Theorem B, it is necessary to consider all integral powers of $\mathcal{L}$ in Theorem A. Otherwise for $z\in\R\setminus(\tau/2)\Z$, if we choose $s_{1},s_{2}\in\R\setminus(\tau/2)\Z$ such that $\gamma(s_{i})\leq\gamma(z)$ for each $i=1,2$ and define $f=\phi_{s_{1}}+\phi_{s_{2}}$ then $f$ satisfies all the hypothesis of Theorem A but $\mathcal{L}f\neq\gamma(z)f$.
nodes.statement_short: $f=\phi_{s_1}+\phi_{s_2}$ satisfies Theorem A's hypotheses for one-sided $k$ yet is not an eigenfunction.
nodes.section: 4 Sharpness of the main results and the case $q=1$

nodes.name: Theorem B fails off the prescribed real parts
nodes.statement: The conclusions of Theorem B, Part $1$ (resp. Part $2$) does not hold for $z=\alpha\pm i\delta_{p^{\prime}}$ where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\setminus (n\tau)\mathbb{Z}$ (resp. $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\setminus ((2n+1)\tau/2)\mathbb{Z}$). The counterexamples can be constructed in a similar way as we did in Lemma B1, part (c).
nodes.statement_short: For $z=\alpha\pm i\delta_{p'}$ with $\alpha$ outside the prescribed lattice, Theorem B fails, as in Lemma B1(c).
nodes.section: 4 Sharpness of the main results and the case $q=1$

nodes.name: Weaker Lorentz norms admit non-eigenfunctions
nodes.statement: In Theorem B (resp. in Theorem A), if we consider $z=\alpha\pm i\delta_{p^{\prime}}$ where $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ (resp. $z\in\R$) and substitute the $L^{p^{\prime},\infty}$ norm (resp. $L^{2,\infty}$) by the $L^{q^{\prime},r}$ where $1\leq q<p<2$ (resp. $L^{p^{\prime},r}$ where $1<p<2$, $1\leq r\leq\infty$ or $L^{\infty}$), then there are functions which satisfies the hypothesis but are not eigenfunctions of $\mathcal L$.
nodes.statement_short: Substituting $L^{q',r}$ or $L^\infty$ norms for the weak-type norms produces functions satisfying the hypotheses but failing to be eigenfunctions.
nodes.section: 4 Sharpness of the main results and the case $q=1$

nodes.name: Motivation for treating the case $q=1$ separately
nodes.statement: Having dealt with all viable generalizations of Roe's result on homogeneous trees of degree $q+1$ where $q\geq 2$, it becomes quite plausible to consider this problem on a homogeneous tree of degree 2 (i.e., when $q=1$), which may be identified to $\mathbb{Z}$. This identification distinguishes it from others in terms of its geometric and analytic properties. However, the most intriguing difference in the context of this article lies in the spectrum of their respective Laplace operators. Hence we deal with this case separately.

nodes.name: Laplace operator $\mathcal{L}_{\mathbb{Z}}$ on $\mathbb{Z}$
nodes.statement: The Laplace operator on $\mathbb{Z}$ is defined as $$\mathcal L_{\mathbb{Z}} f(m)=f(m)-\frac{f(m-1)+f(m+1)}{2}\quad\text{for all }m\in\mathbb{Z}.$$

nodes.name: The spectrum of the Laplacian on $\mathbb{Z}$ is a line segment
nodes.statement: Unlike the spectrum of $\mathcal{L}$ which is a $p$-depend on the elliptic region, the spectrum of $\Delta_{\mathbb{Z}}$ is always a line segment. Having said that, it must also be noted that the term $-2\Delta_{\mathbb{Z}}$ is in some way, a `discrete' representation of the operator $-d^{2}/dx^{2}$ whose spectrum is also a line segment in $\mathbb{R}$. These observations allowed us to use the Fourier transform techniques and motivated us to emphasize an analogy with Roe's result on $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: On $\mathbb{Z}$ the spectrum is always a segment, making $-2\Delta_{\mathbb{Z}}$ a discrete analogue of $-d^2/dx^2$ and Fourier methods available.

nodes.name: Fourier transform on $\mathbb{Z}$
nodes.statement: The Fourier transform $\widehat{f}$ of a finitely supported function $f$ defined on $\mathbb{Z}$, is a function on $\mathbb{T}$ given by $$\widehat{f}(s)=\sum\limits_{m\in\mathbb{Z}}f(m)e^{ims}\quad\text{ where }f(m)=\int\limits_{-\pi}^{\pi}\widehat{f}(s)e^{ims}ds$$ represents it's inverse Fourier transform.

nodes.name: Schwartz space $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{Z})$
nodes.statement: Let us define the Schwartz space $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{Z})=\{f:\mathbb{Z}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}:\lambda_{n}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }n\in\mathbb{N}\}$, equipped with the countable family of semi-norms $\lambda_{n}(f)=\sup(1+|m|)^{n}|f(m)|$.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathbb{T})$ under the Fourier transform
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that the map $f\rightarrow\widehat{f}$ is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{Z})$ onto $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb T)$ where $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb T)=\{g:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}:g\text{ is infintely differentiable on }\mathbb{R},~g(x+\pi)=g(x)\text{ and }\mu_{l}(g)<\infty\text{ for all }x\in\mathbb{R},l\in\mathbb{N}\text{ respectively}\}$ where $\mu_{l}(g)=\sup|g^{(l)}(s)|$ defines a countable family of semi-norms.
nodes.statement_short: The Fourier transform is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{Z})$ onto the smooth $\pi$-periodic functions $\mathcal{C}^\infty(\mathbb{T})$.
conclusions: the map $f\rightarrow\widehat{f}$ is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{Z})$ onto $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(\mathbb T)$

nodes.name: Distributions on $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{Z})$ and their Fourier transform
nodes.statement: Analogous to the Euclidean case, a distribution $T$ is a continuous linear functional on $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{Z})$ whose Fourier transform is defined as $$\langle \widehat{T},\phi\rangle=\langle T,\left(\phi^{\vee}\right)^{\#}\rangle,\text{ where }\widehat{\phi^{\vee}}=\phi\text{ and }\left(\phi^{\vee}\right)^{\#}(m)=\phi^{\vee}(-m).$$

nodes.name: The theorem on $\mathbb{Z}$ follows Roe's argument
nodes.statement: Now we state the Theorem on $\mathbb{Z}$, which can be proved by the similar argument developed by Roe in \cite{R}.

nodes.name: Theorem on $\mathbb{Z}$ (case $q=1$)
nodes.statement: Let $\{f_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be a doubly infinte sequence of functions on $\mathbb{Z}$ which satisfies $\mathcal{L}_{\mathbb{Z}} f_{k}=(1-\cos\alpha)f_{k+1}\quad\text{ for }\alpha\neq 0$ and there exists constants $M_{k}\geq 0$, $\beta\in(0,1]$ and a non-negative integer $n$ such that $|f_{k}(m)|\leq M_{k}(1+|m|)^{n+\beta}\text{ for all }k,m\in\mathbb{Z}.$ If $\liminf\limits_{k\rightarrow \infty}\frac{M_{k}}{(1+\epsilon)^{k}}=0$ and $\liminf\limits_{k\rightarrow \infty}\frac{M_{-k}}{(1+\epsilon)^{k}}=0$ for all $ \epsilon>0$ then $f_{0}(m)=p(m)e^{im\alpha}+q(m)e^{-im\alpha}$ where $p,q$ are polynomials of degree atmost $n$.
nodes.statement_short: On $\mathbb{Z}$, polynomial growth with subexponential $\liminf$ conditions forces $f_0(m)=p(m)e^{im\alpha}+q(m)e^{-im\alpha}$ with $\deg p,q\le n$.
assumptions: there exists constants $M_{k}\geq 0$, $\beta\in(0,1]$ and a non-negative integer $n$ such that $|f_{k}(m)|\leq M_{k}(1+|m|)^{n+\beta}\text{ for all }k,m\in\mathbb{Z}.$
conclusions: $f_{0}(m)=p(m)e^{im\alpha}+q(m)e^{-im\alpha}$ where $p,q$ are polynomials of degree atmost $n$

nodes.name: Extension of the theorem on $\mathbb{Z}$ to $\mathbb{Z}^n$
nodes.statement: We can also extend the above result to $\mathbb{Z}^{n}$ (as done by Strichartz \cite{S}) where the Laplacian is defined as $$\mathcal{L}_{\mathbb{Z}^{n}}f(m)=f(m)-\frac{1}{2n}\sum\limits_{k:|m-k|=1}f(k).$$ But here we assume that $M_{k}$ satisfies a sublinear growth, that is $\lim\limits_{k\rightarrow \pm\infty}\frac{M_{k}}{k}=0$.
nodes.statement_short: The same statement holds on $\mathbb{Z}^n$ under a sublinear growth assumption on $M_k$.

nodes.name: Purpose of the appendix
nodes.statement: To make our exposition self-contained, we now prove the isomorphism theorems for the spherical Fourier transform defined on the space $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ where $1<p\leq 2$. However, the $\mathcal{S}_2(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ isomorphism theorem is already proved in \cite{JF} (see Theorem 3.3).

nodes.name: Spherical Fourier transform via the Abel transform
nodes.statement: Recalling expression (\ref{Equation 2.6}), the spherical Fourier transform of a function $f\in\mathcal{D}(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ can also be written as \begin{equation} \hat{f}(z)=\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathcal{A}f(n)q^{inz}, \end{equation} where $\mathcal{A}f$ denotes the Abel transformation of $f$.
nodes.statement_short: $\hat{f}(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathcal{A}f(n)q^{inz}$, i.e. the spherical transform is the Fourier series of the Abel transform.

nodes.name: Abel transform isomorphism (Cowling, Meda and Setti)
nodes.statement: Cowling et al. proved (see Theorem 2.5, \cite{CMS}) that $f\rightarrow\mathcal{A}f$ is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ onto $q^{-\delta_{p}|\cdot|}S_{ev}(\mathbb{Z})$, for every $p\in(1,2]$ where $S_{ev}(\mathbb{Z})$ is the space of all even functions on $\mathbb{Z}$ such that $\lambda_{m}(F)=\sup\limits_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}(1+|n|)^m|F(n)|<\infty$ for all $m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ and $\lambda_{m}(\cdot)$ defines a countable family of semi-norms on $S_{ev}(\mathbb{Z})$. In fact, for any natural number $m\geq 2$, there exists a constant $C(p,m)>0$ such that for all $f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$, \begin{equation} C^{-1}\lambda_{(m-2)}(q^{\delta_{p}|\cdot|}\mathcal{A}f)\leq\nu_{m}(f)\leq C\lambda_{m}(q^{\delta_{p}|\cdot|}\mathcal{A}f). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The Abel transform is a topological isomorphism $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}\to q^{-\delta_p|\cdot|}S_{ev}(\mathbb{Z})$, with two-sided seminorm bounds.
conclusions: $f\rightarrow\mathcal{A}f$ is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ onto $q^{-\delta_{p}|\cdot|}S_{ev}(\mathbb{Z})$

nodes.name: Sources of the appendix technique
nodes.statement: We use the above result to prove the following isomorphism theorem. Proof of this theorem is influenced by the technique given in \cite{CMS} and \cite{BD}.

nodes.name: $L^p$ isomorphism theorem for the spherical Fourier transform
nodes.statement: The map $f\rightarrow\hat{f}$ is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ onto $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$, for every $p\in(1,2]$.
conclusions: The map $f\rightarrow\hat{f}$ is a topological isomorphism from $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ onto $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$

nodes.statement:

u_{(m+4)}$ of $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ such that, $$\mu_{m}(\hat{f})\leq C
u_{(m+4)}(f)\quad	ext{ for all }f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}.$$ Conversely, assume $g\in\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$. Then for all $r$ with $p<r\leq 2$, the function $g(\cdot+i\delta_{r})$ is an infinitely differentiable function of period $	au$. Hence g has a Fourier series representation of the form $g(s)=\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}F(n)q^{ins}$, where $$F(n)= rac{1}{	au}\int\limits_{-	au/2}^{	au/2}g(s)q^{-ins}ds$$ yields the $n^{	ext{th}}$ Fourier co-efficient of the function $g$. nodes.name: Well-definedness of $\hat{f}$ on $S_p$
nodes.statement: Fix $p\in(1,2)$ (proof of the case $p=2$ is similar). Let $f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ and $z\in S_p$. Then it is clear that the infinite series (\ref{eq15}) converges uniformly on $S_p$ and consequently $\hat{f}$ is well-defined.
nodes.statement_short: The Abel series converges uniformly on $S_p$, so $\hat{f}$ is well-defined there.

nodes.name: Analyticity and the forward seminorm bound
nodes.statement: The analyticity of $\hat{f}$ on $S_p^{\circ}$ follows directly from the analyticity of $q^{inz}$ together with the fact that the infinite series (\ref{eq15}) converges uniformly on any compact subset of $S_p^{o}$. Infact for every $m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$, $$\hat{f}^{(m)}(z)=\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}(in\log q)^m\mathcal{A}f(n)q^{inz},\quad\text{for all } z\in S_p^{o}.$$ The above expression together with equation (\ref{eq16}) implies that for every semi-norm $\mu_{m}$ of $\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$, there exists a semi-norm $\nu_{(m+4)}$ of $\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ such that, $$\mu_{m}(\hat{f})\leq C\nu_{(m+4)}(f)\quad\text{ for all }f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate the series termwise and use the Abel-transform seminorm bounds to get $\mu_m(\hat f)\le C\nu_{m+4}(f)$.

nodes.name: Fourier coefficients of $g$
nodes.statement: Conversely, assume $g\in\mathcal{H}(S_{p})^{\#}$. Then for all $r$ with $p<r\leq 2$, the function $g(\cdot+i\delta_{r})$ is an infinitely differentiable function of period $\tau$. Hence g has a Fourier series representation of the form $g(s)=\sum\limits_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}F(n)q^{ins}$, where $$F(n)=\frac{1}{\tau}\int\limits_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}g(s)q^{-ins}ds$$ yields the $n^{\text{th}}$ Fourier co-efficient of the function $g$.
nodes.statement_short: For $g\in\mathcal{H}(S_p)^{\#}$, expand $g(\cdot+i\delta_r)$ in a Fourier series with coefficients $F(n)$.

nodes.name: Contour shift by Cauchy's integral theorem
nodes.statement: Our aim is to prove that $F\in q^{-\delta_{p}|\cdot|}S_{ev}(\mathbb{Z})$. Applying the Cauchy's integral theorem to $g$, it is easy to verify that for every $r\in(p,2]$ and $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, \begin{align} F(n)&=\frac{1}{\tau}\int\limits_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}g(s+i\delta_{r})q^{-in(s+i\delta_{r})}ds=\frac{1}{\tau}\int\limits_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2}g(s-i\delta_{r})q^{-in(s-i\delta_{r})}ds. \end{align} Infact the first equality in (\ref{eq19}) can be proved using the closed rectangle \begin{multline*} \Gamma(z)=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\Im z=0,-\tau/2\leq \Re z\leq\tau/2\}\cup\{z\in\mathbb{C}: \Re z=\tau/2,0\leq \Im z\leq\delta_{r}\}\\ \cup\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\Im z=\delta_{r},\tau/2\leq \Re z\leq-\tau/2\}\cup\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\Re z=-\tau/2,\delta_{r}\leq \Im z\leq 0\}. \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy's theorem on the closed rectangle $\Gamma(z)$ shows $F(n)$ can be computed on either horizontal line $\Im z=\pm\delta_r$.

nodes.name: Evenness of $F$ and the seminorm bound
nodes.statement: Using the identities (\ref{eq19}) and noting that $g$ is even, one can easily prove that $F(-n)=F(n)$ for all $n\in\mathbb{N}$, that $F$ is even in $\mathbb{Z}$. Integrating by parts the second equation in (\ref{eq19}) (m times) and further using the Dominated convergence theorem and letting $r\rightarrow p$ we have, \begin{equation} \lambda_{m}(q^{\delta_{p}|\cdot|}F)\leq C \mu_{m}(g)\quad\text{for every }m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Evenness of $g$ gives $F(-n)=F(n)$; integrating by parts $m$ times and letting $r\to p$ yields $\lambda_m(q^{\delta_p|\cdot|}F)\le C\mu_m(g)$.

nodes.name: Conclude the inverse bound
nodes.statement: Hence there exists an unique $f\in\mathcal{S}_p(\mathfrak{X})^{\#}$ such that $\mathcal{A}f=F$ and $g=\hat{f}$. Further using equations (\ref{eq16}) and (\ref{eq21}) we conclude that $$\nu_{m}(f)\leq C \mu_{m}(\hat{f})\quad\text{for every }m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.$$ This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Pull $F$ back to a unique $f$ with $\hat f=g$ and obtain $\nu_m(f)\le C\mu_m(\hat f)$.
